in_text_mentions: CD8 + T cells and M1 macrophages (anti-tumor). In contrast, tumors arising from carcinoma cell lines with a mesenchymal phenotype and exhibiting EMT markers expressed low levels of MHC-I, high levels of PD-L1, and contained within their stromal regulatory T cells, M2 macrophages (tumor), and exhausted CD8 + T cells (see Figure 6). Furthermore, mesenchymal carcinoma cells within a tumor retained the ability to protect their epithelial counterparts from immune attack. Finally, epithelial tumors were more susceptible to elimination by immunotherapy than the corresponding mesenchymal tumors [127].

in_text_mentions: and RTU Monoclonal Mouse Anti-human Progesterone receptor (clone PgR 636) were used. IHC was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions. Paraffin-embedded tissue blocks were deparaffinized, sectioned, and stained automatedly. Normal breast tissue was considered a positive control for ER/PR, and staining of more than 1% for ER/PR was considered a positive expression (Figures 1 and 2). Complete membranous expression of HER2/neu in more than 10% invasive cancer cells was considered positive. Cases with equivocal HER2/neu were confirmed using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

panels.figure_caption: A 59-year-old female presented with a palpable mass in her right breast. After undergoing breast conserving surgery, the final pathology report revealed a grade III, ER-negative, PR-negative, and Her-2 positive squamous carcinoma. There were no axillary lymph node metastases identified. (1a-b) Breast MRI showed a dumbbell-shaped, heterogeneously enhancing mass with an irregular shape and margin, located in the upper outer quadrant of right breast. (1c) T2-weighted image showed iso- to hyper signal intensity of the tumor. (1d-e) the diffusion-weighted image showed hyperintensity and the corresponding ADC value showed 1.49x10-3 mm2/s.
in_text_mentions: phology was predominantly mass-type in both groups, with a significant presence in the mesenchymal differentiation group (100% vs. 73.7%). Shape and margins were equally distributed between irregular and round, and circumscribed and irregular, respectively, in the mesenchymal differentiation group, showing no significant difference from the squamous carcinoma group. Kinetic curve assessments in both initial and delayed phases did not significantly differ between the two groups, with most tumors showing fast initial phase kinetics and washout in the delayed phase. (As seen in Table 4, Figs 2–3)

in_text_mentions: and RTU Monoclonal Mouse Anti-human Progesterone receptor (clone PgR 636) were used. IHC was performed according to the manufacturer's instructions. Paraffin-embedded tissue blocks were deparaffinized, sectioned, and stained automatedly. Normal breast tissue was considered a positive control for ER/PR, and staining of more than 1% for ER/PR was considered a positive expression (Figures 1 and 2). Complete membranous expression of HER2/neu in more than 10% invasive cancer cells was considered positive. Cases with equivocal HER2/neu were confirmed using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).

plate_findings.evidence: abundant necrosis and basophilic matrix (caption); malignant neoplasm with a chondroid matrix (in-text)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E stained section of lung metastasis showing chondroid matrix and necrosis, consistent with matrix-producing metaplastic breast carcinoma; article title and caption confirm. [raw subtype: matrix-producing] B: SOX10 immunohistochemistry of lung metastasis showing positive staining in tumor cells, confirming breast origin; part of the diagnostic workup for metaplastic breast carcinoma metastasis. [raw subtype: matrix-producing] C: TRPS1 immunohistochemistry of lung metastasis showing positive nuclear staining, confirming breast origin; supports metastatic metaplastic breast carcinoma. [raw subtype: matrix-producing] D: CK8/18 immunohistochemistry of lung metastasis showing positive cytoplasmic staining, confirming epithelial origin; supports metastatic metaplastic breast carcinoma. [raw subtype: matrix-producing]
panels.attribution_text: Noor et al. Large Solitary Lung Metastasis of a Matrix-Producing Metaplastic Breast Carcinoma: A Diagnostic Challenge.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.50265. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: The metastatic tumor in the lung showed scattered hyperchromatic cells with abundant necrosis and basophilic matrix (A, H&E stain). The tumor cells showed reactivity for SOX10 (B, SOX10 stain, fast red used as chromogen), sensitive breast marker TRPS1 (C, TRPS1 stain, DAB used as chromogen), and cytokeratin (D, CK8/18 stain, DAB used as chromogen), confirming breast as the site of the origin of lung metastatic cancer. H&E: hematoxylin and eosin; DAB: 3,3'-diaminobenzidine.
in_text_mentions: 6.2 cm mass in the lower lobe of her left lung. A CT-guided biopsy of the lung mass showed a malignant neoplasm with a chondroid matrix, identical to the patient’s prior metaplastic carcinoma. The lung lesion showed the same immunoprofile as the prior breast carcinoma (Figure 2). These findings were consistent with metastasis of the patient’s known matrix-producing metaplastic carcinoma. The patient had a large metastatic tumor, the removal of which would require a complete lobectomy with significant morbidity. She is currently receiving chemotherapy (taxane) and immunotherapy (pembrolizumab).

plate_findings.evidence: gross modified radical mastectomy specimen, demonstrating the resected breast tissue and a large tumor with extensive necrotic changes

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Preoperative clinical photograph of the left breast lesion in a case of triple-negative metaplastic breast carcinoma, showing marked erythema and swelling of the overlying skin with ulceration, crust formation and areas suggestive of tumor necrosis, as described in the caption and in-text mentions. No vocabulary finding key matches the cutaneous inflammatory/necrotic presentation, so the visible manifestations are listed as proposed findings. Skin tone assessed from the visible, adequately lit breast skin. B: Gross mastectomy specimen of the same metaplastic breast carcinoma patient, showing a large fleshy tumor with extensive necrosis, matching the vocabulary finding metaplastic_breast_carcinoma_necrotic_tumor_gross. Panel is a real human surgical specimen image directly tied to the target disease by the case report title and caption.
panels.attribution_text: Hu et al. Case Report: Triple-negative metaplastic breast carcinoma with primary resistance to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, refractory tumor necrosis-related fever, and rapid postoperative disease progression.. Frontiers in oncology 2026. doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1943838. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Local presentation of the left breast lesion and surgical specimen. Panel (A) shows the preoperative appearance of the left breast, with marked erythema and swelling of the skin, associated with ulceration, crust formation, and areas suggestive of tumor necrosis. Panel (B) shows the gross modified radical mastectomy specimen, demonstrating the resected breast tissue and a large tumor with extensive necrotic changes. The two panels illustrate the severe local presentation of the breast lesion before surgery and the corresponding gross appearance of the resected specimen.
in_text_mentions: the left breast, the overlying skin was markedly erythematous and swollen, with visible superficial vessels; the skin involvement was less than one-third of the left breast. The central portion of the lesion was elevated, measuring approximately 5 cm × 6 cm, with skin ulceration, crust formation, and increased local skin temperature. A poorly defined mass measuring approximately 6 cm × 5 cm was palpable in the lower inner quadrant, with limited mobility. No other obvious abnormalities were noted on physical examination. Representative clinical and gross surgical findings are shown in Figure 1.

panels.figure_caption: Breast MRI demonstrating an irregular mass (2.6 × 2.2 cm) with skin thickening and chest wall involvement.
in_text_mentions: Breast MRI demonstrated an irregular mass (2.6 x 2.2 cm) in the deep portion of the left breast outer quadrant. The mass showed mixed signal intensity on T2-weighted imaging (heterogeneous iso- to hyperintense), low signal on T1-weighted imaging, high signal on DWI, and slightly low signal on ADC map (ADC value approximately 1.36). The lesion exhibited skin thickening and retraction, involving the adjacent chest wall (Figure 2). Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI showed marked heterogeneous enhancement with time-signal intensity curves showing plateau and washout patterns.

panels.figure_caption: Microscopic evaluation Sections revealed breast parenchyma with an infiltrating tumor composed of nests, irregular cords, and trabeculae. The cells had an abundant cytoplasm and displayed marked nuclear pleomorphism and distinct nucleoli. Areas of squamous differentiation with keratinization and dyskeratotic cells were also seen. Fibrous-appearing stroma was present.
in_text_mentions: After completing chemotherapy, the patient underwent a left modified radical mastectomy. The histopathology report (Figure 4) indicated a 2.2 cm invasive ductal carcinoma with metaplastic features, graded as grade III. The tumor invaded the dermis without skin ulceration. The resection margins were free of tumor, and none of the 13 lymph nodes examined showed evidence of tumor.

panels.rationale: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of a real patient with a circumscribed enhancing left breast mass (arrow), matching the captioned primary tumor of metaplastic breast carcinoma; the article title and in-text mentions attribute the mass to metaplastic breast carcinoma. Axillary nodal metastasis is visible in the caption but not the single displayed slice; subtype not specified.
panels.attribution_text: Kanwal et al. Unraveling Stigmas of Male Breast Carcinoma: A Singular Case of Advanced Metaplastic Breast Carcinoma in a Young Male.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.44174. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Computed tomography for the metastatic workup The left breast demonstrated a large, enhancing circumscribed retroareolar mass measuring 3.4 cm in maximum dimension associated with ipsilateral metastatic axillary node, with the largest having a short axis diameter of 2.5 cm. There was a plump benign-appearing subcarinal lymph node with a short axis diameter of 1.1 cm along with a right hilar subcentimeter calcified node. The visualized lower cervical and the right axilla and supraclavicular recesses were clear. There were no suspicious pulmonary or pleural focal abnormality or effusions. There was no evidence of hepatopulmonary or osseous metastasis.
in_text_mentions: To assess the extent of metastasis, a computed tomography (CT) scan was performed (Figure 3), which revealed a primary mass in the left breast with ipsilateral axillary lymph node involvement. No evidence of metastasis to the liver, lungs, or bones was found.

These tumor nests aggressively invade the surrounding stroma/fat with focal desmoplastic fibrosis. MBC: metaplastic breast carcinoma

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real-patient mammographic craniocaudal view of the right breast mass in a case report of spindle cell metaplastic breast carcinoma; the caption and in-text describe a 55 x 48 mm high-density irregular mass with spiculated margins and architectural disruption (BI-RADS 5), directly supporting the target disease. Irregular spiculated (rather than well-circumscribed) mammographic appearance is a less typical presentation for metaplastic carcinoma, hence variant. [raw subtype: spindle cell metaplastic breast carcinoma] B: Real-patient mammographic mediolateral oblique view of the same right breast mass in the spindle cell metaplastic breast carcinoma case report; caption supports a high-density irregular mass with spiculated margins and local edema, attributable to the target disease. plate_findings.evidence: large, relatively well-demarcated heterogeneous right breast mass occupying most of the breast

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of a patient with metaplastic breast carcinoma shows pathological right axillary and infraclavicular lymph nodes marked by a red arrow; this is a real patient image showing nodal disease, though the specific nodal finding is not in the vocabulary. B: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows the large, relatively well-demarcated heterogeneous right breast mass characteristic of the reported metaplastic breast carcinoma, marked by a red arrow. C: Axial contrast-enhanced CT demonstrates the heterogeneous right breast tumor and its broad posterior contact with the pectoral fascia, consistent with the metaplastic breast carcinoma case. D: Axial contrast-enhanced CT shows the inferior and anterior extent of the large right breast tumor with nipple-areolar involvement, marked by a red arrow.

Synchronous Metaplastic Breast Carcinoma with Mesenchymal Differentiation and Triple-Negative Invasive Papillary Carcinoma: A Case Report and Literature Review. Journal of clinical medicine 2026. panels.figure_caption: Preoperative contrast-enhanced computed tomography findings. (A) Axial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) image at the level of the upper thorax showing pathological right axillary and infraclavicular lymph nodes (red arrow). (B) More caudal axial CT section showing the large, relatively well-demarcated heterogeneous right breast mass occupying most of the breast (red arrow). (C) Axial CT image at the level of the main pulmonary arteries showing heterogeneous internal enhancement of the tumor and broad posterior contact with the pectoral fascia; the red arrow indicates the posterior tumor margin. (D) More caudal axial CT section showing the inferior and anterior extent of the tumor; the red arrow indicates involvement of the nipple–areolar region. No definite intrathoracic metastatic lesions were identified on the preoperative examination.

in_text_mentions: All seven cases had mammograms available for review. Mammographically, the majority presented as a suspicious irregular mass with either spiculated or indistinct margins (n = 5) (Figures 1–4). Only one patient presented as an oval circumscribed mass as seen in majority of the metaplastic literature (Figure 2).1–4 One patient presented as a focal asymmetry, which possibly represented a mass however imaging evaluation of this case was limited as only old mammograms without tomosynthesis were available for review.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a real patient ultrasound showing a hypoechoic irregular breast mass in a case of metaplastic breast carcinoma; the finding matches the provided ultrasound vocabulary. B: Panel B is a real patient gross mastectomy specimen from the reported metaplastic breast carcinoma case. The specific gross appearance is not fully covered by the provided finding vocabulary, so proposed findings are used. C: Panel C is a real patient H&E histology image from the metaplastic breast carcinoma case, showing pleomorphic cells, multinucleated giant cells, and high mitotic activity supported by the caption.
panels.attribution_text: Li et al. Case Report: Metaplastic breast carcinoma with osseous and chondrodifferentiation in liver metastasis: a rare case and review of literature.. Frontiers in oncology 2025. doi:10.3389/fonc.2025.1437887. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Breast mastectomy and H&E staining result of the tumor. (A) Breast US images revealed a hypoechoic irregular mass in the breast left upper quadrant, with a size of about 8.39 × 8.07 × 6.19 cm. (B) Whole excised tissue of the left breast. The mass was completely moved out with breast mastectomy. (C) The tumor was composed of two components: carcinoma and sarcoma components. The tumor cells in the cancer area are epithelial-like, locally nested, nuclear vacuolated, and scattered mitotic images. The tumor cells in the sarcoma area are scattered, of varying sizes, round or oval, and with large, vacuolar nuclei. Multinucleated tumor giant cells are often observed, and mitotic images are more common showing moderate to marked nuclear pleomorphism. Scale bar = 50 µm (H&E, ×200).
in_text_mentions: (CT) examination. Preoperative neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered, consisting of four cycles of epirubicin (100 mg/m2) + cyclophosphamide (600 mg/m2). The color Doppler ultrasound examination indicated no obvious change about the size in the left breast mass. Then, we changed to paclitaxel (175 mg/m2) for two cycles. At re-examination on April 26, 2018 with color Doppler ultrasound, the tumor diameter in the left breast increased to 8.39 × 8.07 × 6.19 cm, with irregular shape, punctiform strong echo, and axillary lymph nodes at 12 × 7 mm ( Figure 2A ). Surgery was performed as decided.

Radical resection of the left breast carcinoma was performed on June 4, 2018. The postoperative pathological examination indicated that the left breast tissue was completely removed ( Figure 2B ). The size of the mass was 8.5 cm × 8.0 cm × 6.2 cm, and the section was gray and slightly hard. The tumor was composed of two components—carcinoma and sarcoma components—displayed with obvious mitotic images and nuclear polymorphism of unusual cellular or stromal components ( Figure 2C ). in_text_mentions: According to their behavior and histopathological features, MBC can be subclassified as high-grade and low-grade [3]. High-grade MBC (HG-MBC) include squamous cell carcinoma (SqCC), spindle cell carcinomas (SpCC), and MBC with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation (MBCHMD). In addition, mixed MBC (MMBC) is composed of more than one subtype (Figure 1). Low-grade MBC are represented by low-grade adenosquamous carcinoma (LGASC) and fibromatosis-like MBC (FLMBC) [1]. In this review, we have focused on HG-MBC.

in_text_mentions: eoperative diagnosis of MBC on core needle biopsy was achieved in five patients (17.9%). In our series, the most common pathological subtype of MBC was biphasic sarcomatoid carcinoma (SC), which was conspicuous in 13 patients (46.4%) (Figures 1, 2). Five patients (17.9%) disclosed MBC with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation (MCHMD) while another five patients (17.9%) exhibited high-grade adenosquamous carcinoma (HGAS). Pure squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) was discernible in four patients (14.3%) (Figure 3), whereas spindle cell carcinoma (SpCC) was observed only in a single patient (3.6%).

panels.figure_caption: Representative histopathological features of metaplastic breast carcinoma. (A) Squamous cell carcinoma type, showing anaplastic tumor cells arranged in nests or sheets with squamous differentiation (HE × 100). (B) Chondroblastic or matrix-producing type, showing carcinomatous epithelial components mixed with chondroblastic or mucoid matrix components (HE × 40). (C) Spindle cell carcinoma with osteoid differentiation, showing atypical spindle-shaped or pleomorphic tumor cells with osteoid matrix formation (HE × 200).
in_text_mentions: Immunohistochemistry showed ER positivity in 1 patient (3.7%) and ER negativity in 26 (96.3%). PR status followed the same distribution, and all 27 tumors (100.0%) were HER2-negative. Ki-67 was ≥ 30% in every case, indicating active proliferation. Squamous cell carcinoma was the leading subtype (14, 51.9%), followed by mixed type (4, 14.8%), sarcomatoid type (4, 14.8%), stromal or osteochondral differentiation (3, 11.1%), and spindle cell carcinoma (2, 7.4%) (Figure 1). Thus, the cohort mainly consisted of triple-negative tumors with high Ki-67 expression and frequent squamous differentiation.

in_text_mentions: eoperative diagnosis of MBC on core needle biopsy was achieved in five patients (17.9%). In our series, the most common pathological subtype of MBC was biphasic sarcomatoid carcinoma (SC), which was conspicuous in 13 patients (46.4%) (Figures 1, 2). Five patients (17.9%) disclosed MBC with heterologous mesenchymal differentiation (MCHMD) while another five patients (17.9%) exhibited high-grade adenosquamous carcinoma (HGAS). Pure squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) was discernible in four patients (14.3%) (Figure 3), whereas spindle cell carcinoma (SpCC) was observed only in a single patient (3.6%).

in_text_mentions: with a grayish peripheral halo in the outer upper quadrant. The lesion had a firm, woody consistency, measuring 1.2 × 1.0 × 0.9 cm. Microscopic examination demonstrated a tumor composed of an admixture of mesenchymal and epithelioid components consisting of osteoid matrix (95%) with multinucleated giant cells resembling osteoclasts, along with chondroid matrix component (2%), and invasive carcinoma of not otherwise specified (NOS), Grade 3 (3%). An extensive component of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with a solid architectural pattern and central comedonecrosis was also present. (Figure 1).

A – Metaplastic breast carcinoma with abundant osteoid formation (H&E, ×100); B – High power view showing osseous differentiation (H&E, ×400); C – Vague fascicles of spindle cells with numerous tumor giant cells (H&E, ×100); D – Numerous osteoclastic giant cells interspersed with malignant cells (H&E, ×400).
in_text_mentions: Focal apocrine change was noted. The malignant stromal component comprised of vague fascicles of spindle-shaped cells exhibiting marked nuclear pleomorphism, atypia, vesicular nuclei, and 1-2 conspicuous nucleoli. Mitosis of 13/10HPF along with many atypical mitotic figures was noted. Many bizarre, multinucleated and osteoclastic giant cells were noted along with extensive osseous differentiation. Large cystic areas were identified, which were lined by atypical pleomorphic cells filled with hemorrhage. Many bony trabeculae were identified with surrounding osteoblastic rimming (Figure 2 and 3).

in_text_mentions: Many proliferating blood vessels were noted interspersed in between the atypical pleomorphic cells highlighted by the CD31 immunohistochemical marker. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated a strong diffuse membranous and cytoplasmic positivity for Cytokeratin (CK) in the DCIS component. p63 was positive in the mesenchymal component and focally positive in the DCIS component. Ki-67 proliferation index was around 8-10%, and the tumor cells were triple-negative for ER, PR, and Her2neu. CD31 was negative in the tumor cells (Figure 4).

panels.figure_caption: Histological features and SATB2 expression in metaplastic carcinoma of the breast. (A) H&E staining at 60× magnification (scale bar = 250 μm) showing osteoid matrix in metaplastic carcinoma. (B) H&E staining at 100× magnification (scale bar = 100 μm) displaying a sarcomatoid component. (C) H&E staining at 100× magnification (scale bar = 100 μm) illustrating the transitional zone between the sarcomatoid area and fibro-osteoid matrix. (D) Immunohistochemical SATB2 staining at 100× magnification (scale bar = 100 μm) demonstrating nuclear positivity in the sarcomatoid tumor cells.
in_text_mentions: The surgical specimen revealed a malignant breast tumor (4.5 x 3 x 3 cm) diagnosed as metaplastic carcinoma with predominant mesenchymal differentiation (heterologous osteosarcoma)(Figure 3). The tumor showed partial degeneration, cystic changes, and scattered minimal lymphocyte infiltration in the stroma, consistent with Miller-Payne Grade 2 response. All margins were negative. All 12 axillary lymph nodes were negative for metastasis.

Immunohistochemistry showed: CKAE1/AE3 (partially +), EMA (partially +), Vimentin (+), GATA3 (partially +), Trps-1 (+), CK5/6 (focally +), P63 (partially +), ER (-), PR (-), HER-2 (0), CD34 (-), SATB2 (+)(Figure 3), S-100 (partially +), SMA (-), desmin (-), beta-Catenin (membranous +), P53 (+++, 90%), Ki-67 (+, 70%)(Figure 4). The SATB2 positivity confirmed osteosarcomatous differentiation (Figure 3) (17). The patient tolerated the treatment well without major complications.Treatment timeline of the patient is showing in picture (Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: H&E panel of a patient tumor showing the sarcomatoid, pleomorphic, giant-cell-rich component of metaplastic breast carcinoma with mesenchymal differentiation. B: H&E panel showing the malignant epithelial component of the same metaplastic breast carcinoma with carcinosarcoma morphology. C: Vimentin immunohistochemistry demonstrates mesenchymal differentiation in the sarcomatoid component of metaplastic breast carcinoma. D: p63 immunohistochemistry in the patient tumor supports focal epithelial differentiation in metaplastic breast carcinoma. E: S100 immunohistochemical staining is shown in the metaplastic breast carcinoma tumor cells; it is an ancillary finding rather than a specific diagnostic feature. F: Ki-67 immunostaining shows high, heterogeneous proliferative activity in the patient's metaplastic breast carcinoma.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of metaplastic breast carcinoma with mesenchymal differentiation showing carcinosarcoma morphology. (A) Sarcomatoid component composed of highly pleomorphic malignant cells, including bizarre and multinucleated tumor giant cells (hematoxylin and eosin [H&E], original magnification ×100). (B) Malignant epithelial component consisting of irregular epithelial structures embedded within the tumor stroma (H&E, original magnification ×100). (C) Diffuse cytoplasmic vimentin immunoreactivity in the sarcomatoid component, supporting mesenchymal differentiation (vimentin immunohistochemistry, original magnification ×100). (D) Focal nuclear p63 immunoreactivity in tumor cells (p63 immunohistochemistry, original magnification ×100). (E) S100 protein immunoreactivity in tumor cells (S100 immunohistochemistry, original magnification ×100). (F) High and heterogeneous proliferative activity demonstrated by Ki-67 immunostaining (Ki-67 immunohistochemistry, original magnification ×100).
in_text_mentions: O terminology, the larger tumor was classified as metaplastic breast carcinoma with mesenchymal differentiation, showing carcinosarcoma morphology, and was composed of approximately 95% sarcomatoid/mesenchymal and 5% epithelial components. The sarcomatous component consisted of highly pleomorphic and frequently bizarre malignant cells, including numerous multinucleated tumor giant cells (Figure 3A). The epithelial component was represented by irregular malignant epithelial structures showing poor ductal differentiation (Figure 3B). Extensive areas of tumor necrosis and hemorrhage were present.

Immunohistochemically, the dominant tumor showed prominent mesenchymal differentiation, with diffuse vimentin expression in the sarcomatous component (Figure 3C), whereas focal pancytokeratin AE1/AE3 and p63 expression supported the presence of epithelial differentiation; representative focal nuclear p63 immunoreactivity is shown in Figure 3D. Additional immunoreactivity for S100 calcium-binding protein (S100) protein (Figure 3E), cluster of differentiation 68 (CD68), and smooth-muscle actin was documented. in_text_mentions: AE3 and p63 were seen in few cells of the same component. Furthermore, S-100 and smooth muscle actin were positive in focal areas and CD68 was positive in osteoclast-like areas. A strong nuclear positivity was found against p53 and Ki-67 antibodies (Figure 3). The immunohistochemical analysis of the mandibular biopsy specimen (Table 1) showed similar findings to those of the breast tumor, except for total negativity of p63 and S-100. Considering the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features, the diagnosis of oral metastasis of the sarcomatous component of MBC was confirmed.

Similar to most cases previously reported in the literature, the present case exhibited a triple-negative immunoprofile and also had a high histological grade, which caused many anomalous immunoexpressions, such as focal positivity to SMA, S-100 antibodies, and coexpression of vimentin and CK AE1/AE3 (1% of the cells) in the sarcomatous component. In addition, p53 and Ki-67 markers showed high proliferative rate in both breast and mandible tumors (Table 1; Figures 2 and 3).
